lines: Register a real socket's own connection attempt directly with a readiness-polling library, naming exactly which operation to watch for, then call poll and wait.
Once that connection actually completes, does a real event come back saying so?
answer: Yes — a genuine readiness event comes back, naming the exact socket that just became ready.
This isn't a guess or a timeout firing blindly. It's a real signal, tied to the specific thing that was registered.

lines: Run it for real: register the connection, call poll, and a writable readiness event comes straight back, naming that exact registered socket.
Register interest, then wait to be tapped on the shoulder — and here, for the first time in this chapter, that tap is the literal thing being measured.
steps.takeaway: Registering interest and polling delivers a real readiness event naming the exact source that became ready, not a guess.

lines: Now register a different socket for exactly the same kind of readiness, except this time, nothing is ever written to it at all. Nothing will ever make it ready.
What does the call to poll actually do in that case?
answer: It simply waits — genuinely, for close to the entire length of time it was told to wait, and then comes back empty.
There's no event to deliver, because nothing ever happened. It doesn't guess, and it doesn't return early.

lines: Measure that wait directly: it comes back after almost exactly the full length of time requested, with no event in it at all.
This is the real mechanism this whole chapter has been calling 'an idle worker parking' — here, it's the literal thing, timed.
steps.takeaway: With nothing ever ready, the call genuinely parks for close to the full timeout — the real mechanism behind an idle worker, not a diagram.

lines: Take the ordinary way of waiting a fixed length of time inside one of these async units of work, and time it precisely from the moment it starts.
Does it actually wake up close to the real length of time requested, or does it just wake up eventually, whenever it happens to get around to it?
answer: It wakes up remarkably close to the real, requested length of time — not immediately, and not noticeably late either.
Something is actually watching the clock and waking it at close to the right moment, not just leaving it to chance.

lines: Measure it precisely: ask for two hundred milliseconds, and it wakes at two hundred and one.
This is the thing that actually calls the wake function at the right moment — the exact mechanism an earlier chapter left entirely unnamed.
steps.takeaway: The timer driver is the thing that actually calls wake at close to the right moment — proven directly here, not assumed.

lines: There's a newer, much-discussed way of doing fast input and output on modern systems that some runtimes have already adopted as their default.
Is that the default way this particular runtime does its input and output now?
answer: No — not by default, and not without explicitly opting into it.
It's real, and it exists, but it's still marked unstable, requiring an explicit flag most programs never pass.

lines: The crate's own words say this plainly: that feature is Linux-only, and using it at all requires passing a specific, explicit flag to the compiler, one that openly admits its own public interface might still change.
Nothing about everything measured so far in this topic depends on it at all.

Put the whole cycle back together now, with every single step of it already backed by something measured directly in this very topic: register interest in something specific, wait, a real event names exactly what became ready, that wakes the right unit of work, and it runs again from there.
An earlier chapter built the waking and polling contract in the abstract, with a hand-rolled, single-threaded stand-in. This is the real thing that calls it, for real, in a real runtime.
Registering interest and polling delivers a real, named readiness event once something genuinely becomes ready.
With nothing ready at all, that same call genuinely parks for the full length of time requested, no shortcuts.
A timer wakes a waiting unit of work close to its real, requested deadline, measured down to the millisecond.
And a newer, faster way of doing input and output exists, named honestly as real but still unstable, not the default.

Every one of these mechanisms, across this entire chapter, is a genuine, working guarantee. And every single one of them can also be broken: a unit of work that never yields, a channel with no real limit on it, a cancellation path nobody ever actually defined.
